title: Universal Screening & Toxicology Testing (Minn. Stat. § 260E.32)
sponsor: Pregnancy Health and Substance Use Workgroup
description:
Repeals the current toxicology-testing mandate in section 260E.32 and replaces it with a universal prenatal and birth screening requirement, moved out of the child protection chapter (260E) and reframed as a health-reporting statute.

Under current law, a physician must administer a toxicology test to a pregnant patient (or a newborn) whenever obstetrical complications suggest possible nonmedical drug use, and a positive result is reported as a neglect referral under 260E.31/260E.03. Testing is therefore targeted, complication-triggered, and wired directly into the child protection reporting pipeline.

**Why it matters:** Tying a medical test directly to a child protection report creates a strong disincentive for pregnant people to disclose substance use or seek prenatal care in the first place — a patient who suspects a positive test could trigger a CPS referral has a reason to avoid care altogether. This proposal breaks that link:

- Replaces targeted, complication-triggered toxicology testing with universal screening (a verbal or written validated tool) for every pregnant or birthing person, with referrals to services based on need rather than a positive drug test
- Makes toxicology testing itself optional and clinical — administered only when it serves a medical purpose in treating the patient or infant, not as a reporting trigger
- Redirects toxicology test reporting to the Department of Health as public health data (protected under section 13.384) instead of automatically routing it through child protection
- Requires confirmatory testing from an accredited laboratory before a positive result can be reported, reducing false positives feeding into the system
- Preserves the existing mandated-reporter duty to report prenatal substance exposure separately, under 260E.03/260E.06/260E.31 — this section stops being the mechanism that does that reporting itself

title: Narrowing the Definition of Prenatal-Exposure Neglect (Minn. Stat. § 260E.03)
sponsor: Pregnancy Health and Substance Use Workgroup
description:
Narrows the statutory definition of "neglect" so that prenatal exposure to alcohol or a controlled substance is only maltreatment if it demonstrably harms the infant — not simply because a test came back positive.

Current law (260E.03, subd. 15(5)) defines prenatal substance exposure itself as neglect, evidenced by withdrawal symptoms, a positive toxicology test, developmental delays, or a fetal alcohol spectrum disorder diagnosis — with no separate requirement that the exposure actually caused harm.

**Why it matters:** Under the current standard, exposure and harm are treated as the same thing, which is the core problem this proposal (together with the 260E.32 rewrite) is designed to fix.

- Rewrites clause (5) so a report of prenatal exposure to alcohol or a controlled substance only counts as neglect when it "adversely affects the infant's health, basic needs, and safety" — exposure alone is no longer sufficient
- Broadens the substance covered from "controlled substance" to "alcohol or a controlled substance" explicitly, and updates the cross-referenced definition from section 253B.02 to section 152.02
- Separately loosens clause (7), the general caregiver substance-misuse standard, from requiring "chronic and severe" use to "chronic or severe" use — lowering the bar for that unrelated category even as clause (5) raises it for prenatal exposure specifically
- Sets up the two-track reporting structure created in the companion changes to 260E.31: harmful exposure becomes a maltreatment report, exposure without demonstrated harm becomes a non-maltreatment safe-care notification

title: Reporting & Response to Prenatal Substance Exposure (Minn. Stat. § 260E.31)
sponsor: Pregnancy Health and Substance Use Workgroup
description:
Rewrites the reporting and response framework for prenatal substance exposure in 260E.31 — replacing a single, CPS-only reporting pipeline with a two-track system, and repealing the mandate that local welfare agencies pursue emergency civil commitment against a pregnant person who declines services.

**Why it matters:** This is the operational heart of the package. Three changes matter most:

- **Removes the mandatory civil commitment trigger.** Current law requires the local welfare agency to seek an emergency admission under section 253B.051 if a pregnant person refuses recommended voluntary services or fails treatment. This proposal deletes that mandate outright, replacing compelled commitment with a voluntary, services-based response — removing what has been one of the most coercive features of current law and a significant deterrent to disclosure.
- **Splits post-birth handling into two tracks.** A "Reports at birth" track continues into the standard child maltreatment process, but only where exposure adversely affects the infant's basic needs and safety (mirroring the narrowed 260E.03 definition). A new "Notification at birth" track routes exposure without demonstrated harm to a state CAPTA portal instead — explicitly not a maltreatment report — aligning Minnesota with the federal Child Abuse Prevention and Treatment Act's Plan of Safe Care notification requirement.
- **Reframes the response to reports made during pregnancy** around a "plan of safe care" — coordinated services (prenatal care, substance use treatment, mental health services, housing, transportation, etc.) for the infant and family — replacing the narrower "offer services indicated under the circumstances" standard, and broadens the mandatory-reporting exemption so a professional coordinating any recommended health care for the patient (not just prenatal care specifically) can avoid triggering a report while treatment continues.

Language throughout the section is also updated from "woman" to "pregnant person," and cross-references are updated to match the revised definitions in 260E.03 and 260E.32.

title: Plug-In Solar Photovoltaic Devices (Minn. Stat. § 216B.2429)
sponsor: Rep. Larry Kraft (DFL-St. Louis Park), with 21 co-authors
description:
Creates a new statute, Minn. Stat. § 216B.2429, establishing a lightweight regulatory category for small, portable "plug-in" solar devices — often called balcony or deck-mounted solar — and exempting qualifying devices from the interconnection-agreement and net metering rules that otherwise apply to anything connected to a customer's home electrical system.

Under current law, any device tied into a customer's electrical system, regardless of size, falls under the same interconnection agreement and net metering framework built for permanent, professionally installed rooftop solar arrays. That process can involve utility approval, inspection, and paperwork that takes weeks — workable for a homeowner installing a full rooftop system, but impractical for a renter or condo resident who wants to plug a small panel into a wall outlet to offset household electricity use. These devices are common in Europe but have had no clear legal pathway in Minnesota.

**Why it matters:** This proposal creates that pathway by treating small, certified plug-in solar devices as categorically different from grid-tied installations, rather than forcing them through a regulatory process designed for a different scale of equipment:

- Defines a "plug-in solar photovoltaic device" as a portable photovoltaic device that primarily offsets a portion of a customer's electricity consumption, has a maximum power output of 1,200 watts, can connect to an on-site energy storage system, and is listed or certified as compliant with interactive plug-in photovoltaic equipment standards by a testing laboratory recognized under OSHA's Nationally Recognized Testing Laboratory program
- Exempts qualifying devices from having to enter an interconnection agreement with an electric utility
- Exempts qualifying devices from Minnesota's net metering provisions under section 216B.164
- Bars electric utilities from imposing any fee, condition, approval, or reporting requirement on a qualifying device's installation or operation
- Shields electric utilities from liability for damage or injury caused by a plug-in solar photovoltaic device
- Is aimed at renters and multifamily-building residents, who typically cannot install traditional rooftop solar because they don't own or control the building's electrical infrastructure

Introduced February 23, 2026, with Rep. Larry Kraft as lead author and 21 co-authors; referred to the House Energy Finance and Policy Committee, with authors continuing to be added through April 22, 2026.

title: Executive Negligence Liability for Large Corporation Violations (proposed Minn. Stat. § 609.672)
description:
**Note: this is an AI-drafted concept bill (generated via MN Legal Librarian) rather than legislation actually introduced at the Capitol — there is no bill number, author, or committee referral.** It's included here as a draft proposal worth tracking, not as pending legislation.

Creates a new criminal statute, Minn. Stat. § 609.672, that holds individual executives of "large corporations" (over $1 billion in annual gross revenue and 1,000+ employees) personally criminally liable for negligent oversight that allows corporate violations to occur — a significant departure from Minnesota's existing corporate-liability framework, which is built around corporate (not individual) liability and a "knowing" mental-state standard rather than negligence.

**Why it matters:** Current Minnesota law (e.g., § 609.671, § 609.284) generally holds the corporation itself liable when an agent commits violations "knowingly," with individual executive liability reserved for cases where the executive personally participated. This proposal instead:

- Creates a standalone crime for executives — officers, directors, managers, or anyone with supervisory authority over compliance, legal, operations, or risk management — who had actual or constructive knowledge that would lead a reasonable person to investigate compliance, and then failed to exercise reasonable care to maintain a compliance program, investigate, report, or correct the violation
- Triggers on a broad set of "qualifying violations": a criminal conviction or plea, a non-prosecution/deferred-prosecution agreement, or a civil settlement/judgment involving harm (health, safety, financial, data, or environmental) to 1% or more of Minnesota's or the U.S. population
- Sets a gross misdemeanor penalty (up to 364 days, $10,000 fine) for a first offense, escalating to a felony (up to 3 years, $50,000 fine) if the violation occurs while the corporation is already operating under a prior conviction, plea, agreement, or settlement for a qualifying violation
- Provides an affirmative due-diligence defense — the executive bears the burden, by a preponderance of the evidence, of proving they ran a reasonable compliance program, resourced it adequately, audited it, and acted on or reported problems
- Sets a five-year statute of limitations running from when the violation is discovered or reasonably should have been discovered, and states that executive liability is independent of the corporation's own liability

The draft itself flags a number of open problems worth weighing before this could be workable law: it uses a negligence standard where existing corporate criminal law uses "knowing," raising mens rea and due process questions; "constructive knowledge" and "reasonable care" are undefined, inviting inconsistent enforcement; the "executive" definition is broad enough to plausibly sweep in mid-level managers; there's no explicit causation requirement linking the executive's negligence to the violation; and it doesn't address interaction with federal prosecution/double jeopardy or with Minnesota's whistleblower protections.
changes:
++Section 1. [FINDINGS AND PURPOSE]++

++The legislature finds that large corporations exercise significant influence over public health, safety, financial security, and personal privacy in Minnesota; that corporate executives bear responsibility for establishing compliance systems and cultures within their organizations; that current Minnesota law does not adequately hold individual executives accountable when their negligent oversight permits widespread corporate violations; that establishing direct criminal liability for executive negligence will incentivize robust compliance programs and deter corporate wrongdoing; and that a due diligence defense will protect executives who take reasonable steps to prevent violations and report misconduct.++

++Section 2. [NEW STATUTE: MINNESOTA STATUTES, CHAPTER 609, SECTION 609.672]++

++Minnesota Statutes is amended by adding a new section to read:++

++609.672 EXECUTIVE NEGLIGENCE; LARGE CORPORATION VIOLATIONS.++

++Subdivision 1. Definitions.++ ++For purposes of this section:++

++(a) "Large corporation" means any corporation, limited liability company, partnership, or other business entity organized under the laws of any state or the United States that (1) had annual gross revenue exceeding $1,000,000,000 during the calendar year in which the violation occurred; and (2) employed at least 1,000 employees at any time during that calendar year.++

++(b) "Executive" means any officer, director, manager, or person with direct supervisory responsibility over compliance, legal, operations, or risk management functions at a large corporation, or any person with authority to approve policies, budgets, or personnel decisions related to regulatory compliance.++

++(c) "Qualifying violation" means any of the following: (1) a criminal conviction of the corporation for any felony or gross misdemeanor offense under Minnesota law or federal law; (2) a plea of guilty or nolo contendere by the corporation to any felony or gross misdemeanor charge; (3) a non-prosecution agreement or deferred prosecution agreement entered into by the corporation with a prosecuting authority; (4) a civil settlement, judgment, or finding of liability involving: (i) harm to the health or safety of 1% or more of Minnesota's population or 1% or more of the United States population; (ii) financial harm to 1% or more of Minnesota's population or 1% or more of the United States population; (iii) unauthorized disclosure, loss, or misuse of personal data of 1% or more of Minnesota's population or 1% or more of the United States population; or (iv) environmental contamination affecting 1% or more of Minnesota's population or 1% or more of the United States population.++

++(d) "Due diligence" means the executive: (1) established, implemented, and actively monitored a reasonable compliance program designed to detect and prevent violations of law; (2) allocated adequate resources, personnel, and authority to compliance functions; (3) conducted or commissioned regular audits, risk assessments, or compliance reviews; (4) took corrective action upon learning of potential violations; or (5) reported the violation to appropriate law enforcement, regulatory agencies, or internal compliance personnel before the violation was discovered through investigation or complaint.++

++Subd. 2. Criminal liability for executive negligence.++ ++An executive of a large corporation is guilty of a crime if: (a) the corporation commits a qualifying violation; (b) the executive had actual or constructive knowledge of facts or circumstances that would lead a reasonable and prudent person in the executive's position to investigate whether the corporation was complying with applicable law; and (c) the executive failed to exercise reasonable care to: (1) establish or maintain a compliance program; (2) investigate potential violations; (3) report known or suspected violations to appropriate personnel or authorities; or (4) take corrective action upon learning of violations.++

++Subd. 3. Penalties.++ ++(a) First offense or large-scale violation. An executive who violates subdivision 2 is guilty of a gross misdemeanor and may be sentenced to imprisonment for not more than 364 days, a fine of not more than $10,000, or both.++

++(b) Repeat offense. An executive who violates subdivision 2 while the corporation is operating under a prior (1) criminal conviction; (2) plea agreement; (3) non-prosecution or deferred prosecution agreement; or (4) civil settlement or judgment arising from a qualifying violation is guilty of a felony and may be sentenced to imprisonment for not more than three years, a fine of not more than $50,000, or both.++

++Subd. 4. Due diligence defense.++ ++An executive is not guilty under subdivision 2 if the executive proves by a preponderance of the evidence that the executive exercised due diligence as defined in subdivision 1, paragraph (d).++

++Subd. 5. Burden of proof.++ ++The prosecution must prove each element of the crime under subdivision 2 beyond a reasonable doubt, except that the defendant bears the burden of proving the due diligence defense by a preponderance of the evidence.++

++Subd. 6. No corporate immunity.++ ++The criminal liability of an executive under this section is independent of and does not preclude criminal, civil, or administrative liability of the corporation itself.++

++Subd. 7. Statute of limitations.++ ++Prosecution under this section must be commenced within five years after the qualifying violation is discovered or reasonably should have been discovered by the prosecuting authority.++

title: Excessive CEO Compensation Tax & Pay-Ratio Disclosure (proposed Minn. Stat. §§ 290.0921, 290.0922, 289A.08)
description:
**Note: this is an AI-drafted concept bill (generated via MN Legal Librarian) rather than legislation actually introduced at the Capitol — the draft itself carries only a placeholder "HF ____" number and no listed author.** It's included here as a draft proposal worth tracking, not as pending legislation.

Creates a progressive corporate franchise tax surcharge tied to a company's CEO-to-median-worker pay ratio, and a parallel disclosure regime requiring most Minnesota corporations to report that ratio to the Department of Revenue every year.

**Why it matters:** Rather than a flat corporate tax change, this ties tax liability directly to internal pay equity, layered on top of Minnesota's existing 5.8% corporate alternative minimum tax:

- Adds a surcharge on Minnesota taxable income that scales with the CEO-to-median-worker pay ratio: zero below 50-to-1, then stepping from 0.5 percentage points at 50-to-1 up to a maximum 5.0 percentage points at 500-to-1 or greater
- Applies to both publicly traded and privately held C corporations subject to Minnesota franchise tax, but exempts corporations with fewer than 50 employees, tax-exempt organizations, S corporations, REITs/regulated investment companies, and financial institutions
- Defines "CEO" as the highest-compensated executive with primary strategic responsibility, and "median worker compensation" as the median total W-2-equivalent compensation (plus fringe benefits) of all other employees, including part-time, temporary, and seasonal workers but excluding contractors
- Requires every covered corporation to disclose its CEO's name, title, and compensation, median worker compensation, employee count used, and the resulting ratio on its Minnesota return, certified by a corporate officer — with a $500/month penalty (capped at $5,000/year) for failure to disclose
- Keeps privately held companies' pay-ratio data confidential (classified as private/nonpublic data), while publicly traded companies' data — already disclosed under SEC rules — may be released publicly; the Department of Revenue may also share data with the legislature and state agencies for policy research
- Separately requires pass-through entities (partnerships, LLCs, S corps) with 50+ employees to report their pay ratio to Revenue, but does not impose the tax surcharge on them — a C-corporation-only surcharge alongside a broader disclosure mandate
- Would apply retroactively to taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2025

The draft flags several unresolved design questions: whether the surcharge is properly integrated into the existing AMT calculation in § 290.0921; how it should interact with other credits under § 290.06; whether classifying private pay-ratio data as "private data on individuals" under the Minnesota Government Data Practices Act is legally sound given it's aggregate corporate (not personal) data; the asymmetry of taxing C corporations but only requiring disclosure (not a surcharge) from pass-through entities; and open questions on valuing equity/deferred compensation, mid-year hires/departures, and foreign subsidiaries' employees.

++SECTION 4. MINNESOTA STATUTES, SECTION 290.0921, IS AMENDED BY ADDING A SUBDIVISION TO READ:++

++Subd. 1b. Excessive CEO compensation tax surcharge.++ ++(a) Calculation of surcharge. For each taxable year, a corporation subject to the franchise tax under this chapter must calculate a surcharge based on its CEO-to-median-worker pay ratio: (1) less than 50-to-1, surcharge is zero; (2) 50-to-1 to under 100-to-1, 0.5 percentage points; (3) 100-to-1 to under 200-to-1, 1.5 percentage points; (4) 200-to-1 to under 300-to-1, 2.5 percentage points; (5) 300-to-1 to under 400-to-1, 3.5 percentage points; (6) 400-to-1 to under 500-to-1, 4.5 percentage points; (7) 500-to-1 or greater, 5.0 percentage points — each applied to Minnesota taxable income.++

++(b) Applicability. The surcharge applies to all corporations subject to the franchise tax, including publicly traded and privately held corporations, regardless of employee count or annual revenue.++

++(c) Exclusions. The surcharge does not apply to: (1) corporations with fewer than 50 employees on the last business day of the taxable year; (2) tax-exempt organizations under section 290.05; (3) S corporations with a valid election under section 290.9725; (4) regulated investment companies or REITs; (5) financial institutions subject to tax under section 290.9101.++

++(d) Calculation of median worker compensation. If the corporation has no employees other than the CEO, median worker compensation is deemed zero and the ratio is undefined; the surcharge does not apply. With one other employee, that employee's compensation is the median. With an even number of other employees, the median is the average of the middle two, ranked lowest to highest; with an odd number, it is the compensation of the middle employee. Compensation of employees employed less than the full taxable year must be annualized based on the rate at separation or hire.++

++(e) Rounding. The ratio must be rounded to the nearest whole number; a ratio exactly halfway between two whole numbers is rounded up.++

++SECTION 5. MINNESOTA STATUTES, CHAPTER 290, IS AMENDED BY ADDING A NEW SECTION TO READ:++

++290.0922 CEO-to-Median-Worker Pay Ratio Disclosure.++

++(a) Disclosure requirement. Every corporation subject to the franchise tax under section 290.06 must disclose its CEO-to-median-worker pay ratio for each taxable year on its Minnesota corporate income tax return or an attached schedule, in the form prescribed by the commissioner of revenue.++

++(b) Applicability. Applies to publicly traded corporations, privately held corporations, and foreign and domestic corporations doing business in Minnesota, regardless of employee count or revenue, except as provided in paragraph (c).++

++(c) Exclusions. Same exclusions as subdivision 1b, paragraph (c): corporations with fewer than 50 employees, tax-exempt organizations, S corporations, REITs/regulated investment companies, and financial institutions.++

++(d) Contents of disclosure. The CEO's name and title; the CEO's total compensation; the median worker compensation; the number of employees used in the calculation; the pay ratio; and a certification by a corporate officer that the information is accurate and complete.++

++(e) Public availability. The commissioner must make disclosures publicly available in aggregated, anonymized form, except the commissioner may share individual corporation data with the corporation itself, with the legislature and state agencies for policy analysis, and publicly traded corporations' data may be disclosed publicly since it is already subject to SEC disclosure rules.++

++(f) Confidentiality. Pay-ratio data for privately held corporations is classified as private data on individuals and nonpublic data under section 13.02, and is not subject to disclosure under the Minnesota Government Data Practices Act except as provided in paragraph (e).++

++(g) Penalties for nondisclosure. $500 per month of noncompliance, not to exceed $5,000 per taxable year, in addition to any other penalties.++

++(h) Commissioner authority. The commissioner may adopt rules on the form of disclosure; calculation of total and median compensation; treatment of stock/option/equity compensation; treatment of employees hired or separated mid-year; treatment of controlled subsidiaries and affiliated entities; treatment of foreign employees and compensation; and penalties for noncompliance.++

++SECTION 6. MINNESOTA STATUTES, SECTION 289A.08, IS AMENDED BY ADDING A SUBDIVISION TO READ:++

++Subd. 7b. Pass-through entity CEO-to-median-worker pay ratio reporting.++ ++(a) Every pass-through entity subject to the pass-through entity tax under subdivision 7a must report its CEO-to-median-worker pay ratio to the commissioner of revenue in the form prescribed.++

++(b) "Pass-through entity" has the meaning given in subdivision 7a; "CEO-to-median-worker pay ratio" has the meaning given in section 290.0922, subdivision (a).++

++(c) Applicability. Applies to all pass-through entities subject to the pass-through entity tax, except those with fewer than 50 employees on the last business day of the taxable year.++

++(d) Use of information. The commissioner may use this information for policy analysis, research, and enforcement, but must maintain confidentiality as provided in section 290.0922, subdivision (f).++

++SECTION 7. EFFECTIVE DATE. This act is effective for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2025.++
